title: Compact conversational fission PRD draft
content:
Goal:
Ship a compact Hosted API surface that enables low-latency conversational flows with fine-grained tool invocation and deterministic structured outputs while keeping SDK ergonomics simple for client teams. This doc collects constraints, example flows, an API sketch, SDK ergonomics proposals, telemetry/SLOs, and an incremental rollout plan.

Motivation / Problem: 
- Customer teams need predictable partial results for streaming UIs and for tool orchestration. Current heuristic partials are noisy for structured pipelines (search, DB writes, code execution).
- Tooling and client libraries should make it easy to declare what counts as a commit point vs. speculative text. Teams today reimplement fragile client side logic for replay/resume and UX glue.
- We want one coherent surface to support: progressive partials (for UX), atomic tool calls (for actions/side effects), and typed/validated JSON fragments for programmatic consumers.

Principles: 
1) Explicitness: make the contract explicit for partial vs committed frames. 2) Minimal client burden: default SDKs encode safe, obvious behavior with opt-in advanced knobs. 3) Observability: every partial, tool invocation, and schema validation must be traceable back to tokens and prompts. 4) Graceful degradation: allow conservative fallback to text-first rendering if structured output fails or times out.

Primary use cases: 
- Conversational assistant issuing external API calls (tool-calls) mid-generation and presenting incremental UI updates while the tool completes.
- Data extraction pipelines that stream validated JSON fragments to downstream consumers and must fail fast on schema mismatches.
- Mobile clients operating in low-bandwidth/high-latency conditions that want early short summaries and later full fidelity.

Non-goals: 
- Not a general workflow engine (we do not try to model complex multi-step durable sagas in this PRD). 
- Not proposing a brand new RPC protocol — this lives on top of the existing REST/streaming socket surfaces.

High-level solution sketch: "Fission frames"
We introduce the notion of a compact generative frame stream composed of three logical frame types emitted in order:
- partial: best-effort textual/structured fragment for progressive UX (may be overwritten by later frames)
- commit: authoritative result that marks an idempotent boundary (e.g., final JSON for an extraction, or an action to execute)
- tool: a structured handshake that indicates a tool call with input, expected outputs, and invocation metadata
Each frame contains a small header with: frame_id, parent_session_id, sequence_number, frame_type, schema_hint (optional), confidence_hint (optional). Frames are newline-delimited JSONL over streaming endpoints and clients SDKs expose higher-level iterators.

Behavioral examples (2 short flows): 
1) Search + cite assistant (mobile):
 - user: "Find sources for climate risk report"
 - server partial frames: emit a short title and progress summary within 80ms
 - server tool frame: issue tool invocation to websearch plugin with canonicalized query and request_id
 - client acknowledges tool frame and shows a live spinner keyed to tool request_id
 - tool returns results; runtime emits commit frame with validated citations as JSON array (schema: citations.v1). Client swaps the partial rendering for commit rendering.

2) Structured data extraction (backend):
 - client streams a long document; model returns repeated partial frames with candidate records
 - until model emits commit frame with records array and signature hash; SDK validates records against provided JSON Schema; if validation fails, the SDK emits a validation_error event and continues to request a reparse attempt.

API surface sketches:
- REST streaming: POST /v1/responses: body includes conversation_id, streaming=true, schema_tolerance: [strict|lenient|none], tool_policy: [auto|confirm|none]. Response is text/event-stream / application/json-stream with JSONL frames.
- Synchronous convenience: POST /v1/responses?sync=true returns last commit frame (useful for server-to-server where streaming not needed).
- Websocket: same frame envelope over WS messages with small binary optimization for large attachments.

Frame envelope JSON example (single-line):
{ "frame_id": "f-31a4", "session_id": "s-99", "seq": 12, "type": "tool", "schema_hint": "search.query.v2", "payload": {"tool":"websearch","args":{"q":"climate risk models"}}, "meta": {"latency_budget_ms": 250}}

Tool invocation semantics:
- A tool frame is a declarative intent. By default hosted runtime will not execute tool side-effects; it emits a tool frame describing the call and waits for the SDK/client to request execution via a follow-up native-tool-ack frame or the user can opt into runtime-triggered execution with explicit enterprise consent.
- Tool frames are idempotent via request_id (client/runtime ensure dedupe).
- Security: tool arguments are redacted in logs unless the tenant opts in. Tool manifests (allowed inputs/outputs) must be supplied at model registration time in Dedicated and Private deployments.

SDK ergonomics (JS and Python priority):
Defaults we want for 0-config ergonomics:
- read_stream(respones_stream): yields PartialFrame objects until CommitFrame encountered. PartialFrame.text is already sanitized for UI; CommitFrame.payload contains structured JSON if provided.
- tool_handler decorator (JS/Python): canonicalizes a tool manifest into a typed function wrapper that expects commit/confirm semantics.
- resumable_session(session_id): SDK handles socket reconnects, sequence reconciliation, and local speculative state. Exposes a small callback API: on_partial(partial), on_tool(tool_descriptor), on_commit(commit).
- validation hooks: SDK performs best-effort JSON Schema validation against schema_hint and surfaces errors via on_validation_error.

Ergonomic examples: JS pseudo-code
const s = await client.openStream({session: 's-1'});
s.onPartial(p => renderPreview(p.text));
s.onTool(t => showToolPanel(t));
s.onCommit(c => applyStructuredResult(c.payload));

Edge cases and degradations:
- If schema validation times out, emit a commit with status: "fidelity_degraded" and include a textual fallback.
- If tool ack never arrives, SDK auto-fails tool after configurable timeout and emits a recovery_suggestion partial.

Observability / telemetry / SLOs:
- Emit token-level latency histograms: first-partial P50/P95 (target 80ms/300ms), commit P50/P95 (target 150ms/600ms) for small requests (<=512 tokens).
- Track frame loss/reorder metrics per session for socket traffic.
- Schema_validation_rate, schema_validation_fail_rate, tool_invocation_fail_rate, tool_roundtrip_ms.
- Logging: store only schema_hint & hashes for privacy by default; arguments redacted unless tenant allows.

Security and compliance notes:
- For Private deployments: tool manifests must be registered, and tool execution cannot be permitted by runtime by default.
- Provide KMS/HSM hooks for signing commit frames when a tenant needs non-repudiation for data extraction results.

Backward compatibility & migration: 
- Provide a compatibility flag on responses: frame_mode: "legacy" will return a single final result as today. New clients opt-in to streaming frames.
- Gradual rollout: start with internal beta customers + Redwood labs integrations, then open to general beta.

Operational plan / rollout milestones: 
1) Internals-only alpha: wire frame envelope at runtime + primitive JS SDK iteration (2 sprints).
2) Closed beta with 3 customers (e.g., search integrations, CS automation, and one mobile customer) — add tool ack flow and schema validation (4–6 weeks).
3) Public beta: document SDK patterns and telemetry dashboards + adjustable defaults.
4) GA: SLA targets, schema signing, and enterprise tool manifest controls.

Open questions / risks: 
- Should the runtime be allowed to execute tools automatically for hosted customers with an opt-in switch? (privacy/regulatory risk).
- What is the canonical JSON Schema transport format for large nested tool outputs? (need decision between JSON Schema draft-7 vs. lightweight custom type hints).
- How to expose partial confidence so clients can visually de-emphasize low-confidence partials without causing UX jitter?

Next steps: 
- Schedule working session with serving-runtime (Marcus), SDK (Sofia), security (Jae) to align enforcement for tool manifests and redaction policy (week of 2025-01-20).
- Prototype JS SDK streaming iterator and a sample mobile preview component.
- Build a small synthetic load test that measures first-partial latency after enabling frame routing in the runtime.

Notes to reviewers: this is intentionally pragmatic: prefer small explicit primitives rather than a heavy protocol. Feedback requested on the tool-execution default (runtime vs client) and on the schema validation failure modes.
